one_liner: CGO 2018 AVX-512 SpMV format for Xeon Phi Knights Landing that beats MKL CSR SpMV, especially on scale-free graphs.
what_it_does: CVR (Compressed Vectorization-oriented sparse Row) is a sparse-matrix storage format plus a double-precision OpenMP SpMV kernel, shipped as the CGO'18 artifact. The repository is one monolithic benchmark program (spmv.cpp, about 1,950 lines) whose main() reads a Matrix Market file, converts CSR to CVR (pre_processing), runs N SpMV iterations (spmv_compute_kernel), checks the result against a scalar CSR reference and prints preprocessing time, average SpMV time and throughput. There is no library API: using it means extracting those two functions, which take about 20 raw-pointer and size arguments each.
how_it_is_fast: Each SIMD lane owns one row at a time (8 lanes for double on AVX-512), so a single 512-bit fused multiply-add advances 8 rows at once and the per-row reduction disappears; when a lane's row ends, a 'tracker' is fed the next non-empty row, and once rows run out, empty trackers steal nonzeros from longer ones to keep lanes balanced. Conversion records (position, write-back row) pairs in a rec vector so results are written to y at the right point during the streaming kernel. Processing many rows together improves reuse of x; the paper reports an order-of-magnitude lower L2 miss ratio than the other formats and the cheapest conversion (median 2.14 MKL-iterations to amortize on scale-free matrices, versus 5.36 for CSR5 and 49-2,653 for CSR(I), ESB and VHCC).
when_to_use: You still run Xeon Phi Knights Landing (AVX-512 MIC, MCDRAM in flat mode) and need double-precision SpMV on power-law matrices: web graphs, social, wiki, routing and FSM matrices, where the paper's domain averages were 2.5-6.3x MKL.
Iterative solvers or graph kernels running tens to thousands of SpMVs on the same matrix, where CVR's low conversion cost (often under ten iterations to amortize, per the paper) matters.
Matrices with many very short rows (for example ins2 at 4 nnz/row, 17.58x over MKL), where row-per-lane packing keeps all 8 lanes busy.
As a reference design for row-per-SIMD-lane SpMV with feeding and stealing, to port to current AVX-512 Xeons, ARM SVE or GPUs (the authors planned a CUDA/OpenCL port that never appeared in the repo).
when_not_to_use: Any non-KNL machine: the artifact appendix says CVR 'only supports Xeon Phi currently', the Makefile hard-codes icpc -xMIC-AVX512, and Intel has discontinued both KNL and the classic icpc compiler.
Wide, short-and-fat matrices with hundreds or thousands of nonzeros per row (connectus, 12month1, rail4284 in the paper), where VHCC's 2D jagged partition beat CVR.
Regular FEM/HPC matrices where you already use MKL or CSR5: the paper's HPC average is only 1.24x over MKL and 1.10x over the next best format.
Single precision, complex values, transposed products or multi-vector SpMM: the build is double-only (FLOAT_TYPE fixed to double) and only y = A*x is implemented.
Production use: research code with leftover debug printing, a single 2018 code drop, no tests beyond the built-in result check, and no issues or maintainer activity since then.

integration.dependencies: OpenMP; Intel C/C++ compiler 17 with AVX-512; numactl to place data in MCDRAM; Intel MKL only for the prebuilt comparison binaries
integration.min_toolchain: icpc 17.04 (-O3 -xMIC-AVX512 -qopenmp); building with GCC or Clang is not documented
integration.platforms: x86-64 Xeon Phi Knights Landing only (AVX-512F/PF/ER, MCDRAM flat mode); Linux (CentOS 7.3 tested)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the kernel spreads one matrix over OpenMP threads and merges rows split between threads with omp atomic adds

gotchas: Conversion allocates a second copy of values and int32 column indices (nnz entries each) plus a rec array of about 2 x numRows ints, so memory is roughly double the CSR footprint while both exist; all indices are 32-bit, and a kernel comment notes the padded tail uses column 0 with value 0.

The kernel uses _mm512_permute4f128_epi32 and _mm512_i32logather_pd and the Intel-specific '#pragma noprefetch', which tie it to the Intel classic compiler; expect porting work before it compiles elsewhere.
The printed throughput is nnz divided by time, i.e. one flop per nonzero rather than the usual 2*nnz, so its GFlop/s figures are half what most SpMV papers would report for the same time.

The MKL, CSR(I) and ESB comparison programs ship only as binaries (sources withheld over licensing), and every method's SMT thread count was tuned separately, so the baseline side cannot be audited or rebuilt.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose CVR over CSR5 or merge-spmv only on Knights Landing with scale-free matrices, where the paper measured 1.33x average over the best competitor (usually CSR5); on current AVX-512 or ARM SVE CPUs, SPC5 (maintained, block-based, MKL baseline) or CSR5/merge-spmv (portable, CPU and GPU) are the practical picks, and ALBUS targets MKL on regular matrices on Haswell-era Xeons.
verified_claims_summary: On a Xeon Phi 7250 (68 cores, MCDRAM flat mode, icpc 17.04 -O3, 1000 iterations, best SMT thread count per method), double-precision CVR SpMV averaged 2.84x MKL CSR (up to 39.53x on wiki-talk) on 30 scale-free matrices and 1.22-1.24x MKL (up to 17.58x on ins2) on 28 HPC matrices, and 1.33x / 1.10x over the best of CSR(I), ESB, VHCC and CSR5; these are the authors' own peer-reviewed numbers.
status_note: Dormant since 2018 apart from a 2024 README edit (24 stars, MIT), so it is copyable but effectively frozen to discontinued Knights Landing hardware and the Intel classic compiler.
